subcategory: rare San Diego coastal pine tree

planting.note: Start seed in deep pots or plant young container nursery stock in fall through early spring, into lean, fast-draining sandstone or sandy soil in full sun; this pine resents root disturbance, so transplant only while small.

directions: Torrey Pine is one of the rarest native pines in North America, confined in the wild to a few bluffs near Del Mar and Santa Rosa Island, yet it grows readily from seed in cultivated gardens along the Southern California coast. Give it lean, sharply drained soil and avoid summer irrigation once established, since overwatering and rich soil shorten its life and invite root disease. The long, twisted gray-green needles and irregular, windswept silhouette give it strong sculptural character even as a young tree. Choose a permanent planting site carefully, since the long taproot makes this species difficult to relocate after its first year or two.
sources: Torrey Pines State Natural Reserve interpretive materials

subcategory: San Diego coastal bluff evergreen shrub

planting.note: Plant container stock in fall to take advantage of winter rains, into lean, well-drained clay or sandy soil in full sun; seed benefits from hot water or smoke treatment before sowing to break dormancy.

directions: Wart-stem Ceanothus is named for the small, warty bumps studding its rigid, gray-green stems, and is restricted in the wild to coastal bluffs and mesas around San Diego and northern Baja California. Clouds of small white flowers cover the shrub in late winter, drawing large numbers of native bees just as little else is blooming along the coast. It is markedly more tolerant of heavy clay and summer humidity near the ocean than many inland ceanothus species, making it a dependable choice for coastal gardens. Avoid summer water and heavy fertilization, both of which shorten the lifespan of established plants.

subcategory: San Diego coastal sage scrub aromatic shrub

planting.note: Plant container nursery stock in fall through winter into lean, rocky or sandy, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; this slow-growing shrub needs no irrigation once established on a coastal bluff site.

directions: Bush Rue is a dense, rounded, citrus-scented shrub of San Diego coastal sage scrub and chaparral, its small leathery leaves releasing a strong lemony fragrance when crushed, a legacy of its membership in the citrus family. Tiny white flowers appear in late winter and spring, followed by small round fruits that persist into summer. It is exceptionally tolerant of salt spray, poor rocky soil, and long dry summers, making it a durable low shrub for the front of a dry coastal border. Prune only lightly to maintain its naturally tidy mounded form, since it resents hard cutback.
sources: San Diego Natural History Museum flora records

subcategory: San Diego coastal sage scrub evergreen shrub

planting.note: Plant container stock in fall or early winter into lean, rocky, well-drained soil in full sun; seed requires scarification and is slow and erratic to germinate, so most gardeners start from nursery-grown plants.

directions: Mission Manzanita is a true manzanita relative, closely allied to Arctostaphylos, forming a dense evergreen shrub with smooth reddish bark and leathery leaves that are pale green above and whitish-felted beneath, giving the plant its two-toned common name. Clusters of small urn-shaped pink to white flowers open in winter, followed by hard reddish-brown berries favored by birds. It is one of the most drought- and heat-tolerant coastal sage scrub shrubs, surviving on rainfall alone once its deep root system is established over two or three seasons. Give it excellent drainage and resist the temptation to irrigate or feed it, since overly generous care encourages root rot.

planting.note: Root pads from single, healed-off sections in spring or summer directly in lean, sandy or rocky, sharply drained soil in full sun; established plants need no supplemental water beyond rare established-season irrigation.

directions: Coast Prickly Pear sprawls low across sandy coastal bluffs and mesas from Santa Barbara to northern Baja California, its flattened blue-green pads studded with clusters of sharp spines and fine, irritating glochids that call for thick gloves when handling. Bright yellow to apricot flowers open in late spring, followed by reddish-purple fruit that ripens in summer and is edible once the glochids are carefully removed or singed off. It thrives in pure sand or decomposed sandstone with zero summer water and makes an excellent, long-lived barrier planting along an open dry slope. Site it well away from foot traffic paths, since dropped pads root readily and spread over time.

planting.note: Direct sow or plant small container stock in fall, into average to sandy, well-drained soil in full sun; this fast-growing shrub tolerates salt spray, clay, and disturbed ground better than most coastal sage scrub natives.

directions: Coast Goldenbush is a compact, resinous-leaved subshrub of California's coastal bluffs and salt marsh margins, covering itself in masses of small, bright yellow daisy flowers from late summer into fall when most other coastal natives have finished blooming. Its tolerance of salty, poorly drained, or disturbed soils makes it valuable for difficult sites near the immediate coast where few other flowering shrubs persist. The late-season bloom is an important nectar source for migrating butterflies and native bees heading south in autumn. Cut back lightly after flowering to keep the naturally sprawling form tidy and encourage fresh growth.

subcategory: Southern California coastal sage scrub shrub

planting.note: Plant container stock or direct sow scarified seed in fall into well-drained, average soil in full sun; this shrub is frost-sensitive and best limited to mild, near-coastal gardens below about 2,000 feet elevation.

directions: Laurel Sumac is a large, fast-growing, rounded evergreen shrub that dominates lower-elevation coastal sage scrub and chaparral across Southern California, instantly recognizable by its glossy, folded, taco-shaped leaves and a scent often likened to green apple or bitter almond when crushed. Although it was historically classified with poison oak in the genus Rhus and later Toxicodendron, Laurel Sumac is not related to poison oak in any way that causes skin irritation and is entirely safe to handle. Small white flower clusters in early summer give way to small white berries relished by birds, and the shrub's frost sensitivity makes it a useful natural indicator of the mildest microclimates in a garden. Give it room to reach full size and avoid summer irrigation once roots are established.

subcategory: Southern California coastal sage scrub oak shrub

planting.note: Direct sow fresh acorns in fall at about 1 inch depth into well-drained, lean soil in full sun to light shade; buy plants only from growers who verify true Quercus dumosa, since nursery stock is frequently mislabeled or hybridized with the more common inland scrub oak Quercus berberidifolia.

directions: Nuttall's Scrub Oak is a true, narrowly distributed coastal species restricted to maritime sage scrub and chaparral within a few miles of the ocean from Santa Barbara to northern Baja California, distinct from the much more widespread and commonly sold inland scrub oak Quercus berberidifolia with which it has long been confused in both herbaria and nurseries. Its small, holly-like, spiny-toothed evergreen leaves and dense, rounded form make a tough, drought-proof screening shrub for a true coastal garden. Acorns mature in one season and provide food for jays, woodpeckers, and small mammals. Because of the ongoing taxonomic confusion with its inland relative, seek out plants grown from seed collected at known coastal populations if provenance matters for your planting goals.

subcategory: California chaparral and coastal bluff shrub

planting.note: Plant container stock or direct sow in fall into lean, rocky or sandy, sharply drained soil in full sun; chamise is highly flammable and resinous, so keep it well clear of structures in fire-prone landscapes.

directions: Chamise, also called greasewood, is the single most widespread and dominant shrub of California chaparral, forming vast, nearly pure stands on dry slopes and bluffs from the coast to the foothills. Clusters of fine, needle-like leaves cover wiry stems, and in late spring the entire shrub is blanketed in creamy white flower clusters that fade to persistent rust-brown seed heads. It is extraordinarily drought-tolerant, resprouting vigorously from a woody burl after fire, and asks for nothing beyond lean soil and full sun once established. Because of its resinous foliage and tendency to accumulate dead wood, give it generous clearance from buildings and group it only with other low-water, fire-adapted natives.

planting.note: Direct sow or plant small container stock in fall into lean, well-drained, rocky or sandy soil in full sun; this subshrub needs little care once established on an open coastal slope.

directions: Saw-toothed Goldenbush takes its common name from the sharply serrated, resinous leaf margins that distinguish it from other coastal goldenbushes, and it occupies dry bluffs, rocky slopes, and disturbed sage scrub openings along the Southern California coast. Bright yellow, spiky-bracted flower heads open in late summer and fall, providing one of the last significant nectar sources for native bees and butterflies before winter. It is tough and undemanding, tolerating poor rocky soil, wind, and salt air with no irrigation once roots are established. Shear lightly in late fall after bloom to keep the mounding form compact and encourage fresh spring foliage.

subcategory: Southern California coastal sage scrub aromatic shrub

planting.note: Plant container stock or direct sow in fall into average, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; pinch tips of young plants to encourage bushy, floriferous growth.

directions: Fragrant Pitcher Sage is a soft-wooded, gray-green aromatic shrub endemic to the coastal sage scrub of the Southern California and northern Baja California coast, named for its distinctive pitcher-shaped calyx that persists after the pale pink to lavender tubular flowers fade. Crushed foliage releases a strong, resinous fragrance distinct from true Salvia sages, though it shares the mint family's square stems and blooms heavily from spring into summer, attracting hummingbirds and native bees. It is faster-growing and somewhat shorter-lived than many coastal sage scrub shrubs, often needing replacement or renewal pruning after six to eight years. Cut back hard after flowering to maintain a dense, compact shape and extend its productive life.

subcategory: California coastal sage scrub and chaparral wildflower

planting.note: Plant container stock or direct sow in fall or early spring into average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; site away from children and pets since the unripe berries are toxic if eaten.

directions: Purple Nightshade produces clusters of violet-blue, star-shaped flowers with bright yellow anther centers nearly year-round in mild coastal climates, scrambling loosely through sage scrub, chaparral openings, and coastal bluff edges across much of California. Like other members of the nightshade family, its small round berries contain solanine and are toxic to humans and pets if eaten, especially before they ripen, so it is best sited away from areas frequented by young children, dogs, or grazing animals. The sprawling, semi-woody stems benefit from light support or association with neighboring shrubs, and the plant tolerates both full coastal sun and the dappled shade of oak or chaparral edges. Cut back stems that die back after cold winters, since fresh growth readily resprouts from the woody base in spring.
